15.title: slow, on purpose, going nowhere
15.howItsDone: Buddhists practice walking meditation on a set path, walking slowly back and forth while paying attention to each step; on retreats it alternates with sitting, and in Zen halls a slow walk called kinhin comes between periods of zazen.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dana, generosity, the practice taught first. Your line was give first. What did you give before you asked for anything? Day fifteen.

Think about how you walked today. To the car, to the kitchen, down a hallway at work. Probably fast, probably on your phone, probably already thinking about where you were going. Walking, for most of us, is the dead time between places. Now picture a monastery courtyard. A row of people are walking so slowly it almost looks like a film on pause. Lift. Move. Place. Lift. Move. Place. Ten steps up a path, turn around, ten steps back. They aren't going anywhere. That's the point. Today, the other way the Buddha meditated.
screen: `WALKING: DEAD TIME BETWEEN PLACES.` → `A COURTYARD, ALMOST PAUSED.` → `GOING NOWHERE, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Walking meditation. People think of Buddhist meditation as sitting, and it mostly is. But the discourses show the Buddha and his monks walking, too, up and down a set path, often in the evening or before dawn. The Pali word for that path is cankama, a walkway. Monasteries built them: a straight strip of ground, sometimes paved, where you walk back and forth. The Buddha is remembered listing five good things that come from it. You can endure long journeys. You can endure hard effort. It's good for your health. It helps you digest your food. And the calm you find while walking lasts a long time. That last one matters. A calm you find sitting perfectly still can vanish the moment you stand up. A calm you find while moving comes with you. It's already used to your legs. So how is it done? It's simple, and it's not about getting anywhere. You walk slowly and you feel it. The heel lifting. The foot swinging. The weight shifting. The foot touching down. When your mind drifts, you notice, and you come back to the foot. When you reach the end of your path, you stop, turn, and start again. In Zen halls, between long sits, people walk together in a slow line, a practice called kinhin. The Vietnamese teacher Thich Nhat Hanh taught walking as a way of arriving: not walking to get somewhere, but being fully somewhere with every step. Which turns the whole idea of walking upside down. The destination isn't the point. The step is. Every step arrives.
screen: `CANKAMA — A WALKWAY.` · `FIVE GOOD THINGS FROM WALKING.` · `LIFT, MOVE, PLACE.` · `KINHIN, BETWEEN THE SITS.` · then, large: `EVERY STEP ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds. If you can, stand up. Find a few feet of floor. Walk as slowly as you can: lift, move, place. Feel the heel, the sole, the weight. At the end, stop, turn, and walk back. If you can't stand, that's fine: sit, and slowly lift and lower one foot, or just feel your feet resting on the floor. Either way, you're going nowhere, and that's the whole practice. The bell holds the time.
Walking meditation. Slow, on purpose, going nowhere, feeling each step, so the calm can come with you. Fifteenth word.
Your line: every step arrives. Pick one short walk today, to the mailbox, down a hallway, and walk it slowly, feeling each step, phone in your pocket. Day fifteen.

16.title: compassion
16.hook: compassion — metta when it meets pain
16.howItsDone: Buddhists cultivate karuna in meditation, extending the wish that beings be free from suffering, and in action: caring for the sick, the poor and animals; in Mahayana traditions many recite the names or mantra of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion.

segments.voice: Yesterday: walking meditation, slow, on purpose, going nowhere. Your line was every step arrives. Did one short walk get slowed down? Day sixteen.

A friend calls, and you can hear right away that something's wrong. Your first instinct might be to fix it. Give advice. Find the silver lining. Change the subject to something lighter. Or maybe the instinct is to back away a little, because their pain is heavy and you have your own day. Both are normal. Both are ways of leaving. There's a third thing a person can do, and it's much harder than fixing or leaving. You can stay. Remember metta, from day one, the wish for anyone's good? Today, what metta becomes when it meets pain.
screen: `A FRIEND CALLS, SOMETHING'S WRONG.` → `FIX IT, OR BACK AWAY.` → `OR: STAY.`

segments.voice: Karuna. Compassion. It's the second of four qualities Buddhists call the brahmaviharas, the divine abodes, the best places a heart can live. Metta, friendliness. Karuna, compassion. Mudita, gladness at others' good fortune. And upekkha, a steady calm, which you'll meet in a few days. Metta wishes someone well. Karuna is what happens when that wish runs into someone's pain. An old commentary explains the word beautifully: compassion is what makes a good heart tremble when it sees someone suffer. It doesn't turn away. It quivers, and stays. The same commentary warns about two traps. Compassion's far enemy is cruelty, which is obvious. Its near enemy is pity, which is sneaky. Pity looks down: oh, you poor thing, I'm glad that isn't me. Compassion stands beside. The difference is where you're standing. There's a story in the monastic rules about this. The Buddha and his attendant Ananda find a monk lying sick in his own filth, and nobody is caring for him. The Buddha washes him himself, with Ananda's help. Then he gathers the monks and says, in effect: you have no mother or father here to care for you. If you don't care for each other, who will? Whoever would care for me should care for the sick. Across Buddhist traditions, compassion has many faces. In Mahayana Buddhism it's embodied by Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva who hears the cries of the world, known as Guanyin in China and Chenrezig in Tibet. But in every tradition it starts the same way. Someone is hurting. You don't look away.
screen: `KARUNA — METTA MEETS PAIN.` · `THE HEART TREMBLES, AND STAYS.` · `PITY LOOKS DOWN. COMPASSION BESIDE.` · `THE BUDDHA WASHES THE SICK MONK.` · then, large: `STAY.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds. Think of someone who's hurting right now. Someone you know, or someone you saw on the news. Let yourself feel a little of it. Not all of it, just enough that your heart moves. Notice any urge to fix it, or to pull away. Don't act on either. Just stay with them in your mind, breathing. If you like, let a wish go toward them: may you be free from this pain. The bell holds the time.
Karuna. Compassion: metta when it meets pain, the heart that trembles and stays beside, not above. Sixteenth word.
Your line: stay. Today, when someone tells you about something hard, resist fixing it for one whole minute. Just listen, and stay. Day sixteen.

17.title: the community
17.hook: the community; why the Buddha said it's the whole of the path
17.tomorrow: the Buddha's past lives as animals
17.howItsDone: Buddhists take refuge in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, often by reciting the three refuges in Pali; they support monastic communities with food and gifts, and gather with lay sanghas to meditate, chant, study and celebrate festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday: karuna, compassion, metta meeting pain. Your line was stay. Did you listen for one whole minute without fixing? Day seventeen.

Think about the last time you tried to change a habit alone. Going to the gym, eating better, going to bed earlier, meditating every day. For a week, it went great. Then it quietly didn't. Now think about something you actually kept doing. There's a decent chance someone else was involved. A running partner. A class. A friend who texted, you coming? People are strange that way. We can do almost anything together that we can't do alone. The Buddha knew it. And when his closest companion suggested friends were half the path, he corrected him.
screen: `THE HABIT YOU TRIED ALONE.` → `THE ONE YOU KEPT.` → `SOMEONE ELSE WAS INVOLVED.`

segments.voice: Sangha. The word means an assembly, a gathering, a community. It's one of the three things Buddhists take refuge in, called the three jewels. The Buddha, the teacher. The Dhamma, the teaching. And the Sangha, the community that practices it. In its narrowest sense, the sangha means the monks and nuns. The Buddha is remembered describing a fourfold assembly: monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen. Today many Buddhists, especially in the West, use sangha for any group that practices together: a temple congregation, a Tuesday-night sitting group, the people you meditate with online. Here's the story from the discourses. Ananda, the Buddha's cousin and attendant for decades, says to him one day: it seems to me that good friendship is half of the holy life. And the Buddha answers: don't say that, Ananda. Good friendship, good companionship, is the whole of the holy life. Not half. The whole thing. He explains that a person with good friends can be expected to develop the whole path. The friend doesn't replace the practice. The friend is how the practice keeps going. When the Victorian scholar Max Müller translated the Dhammapada in eighteen eighty-one, he rendered sangha with a very English word: the Church. It's a clumsy fit in some ways, but it catches something true. A sangha isn't a club you join because you already agree. It's the people who keep walking beside you on the days you'd rather quit. You need people.
screen: `SANGHA — THE COMMUNITY.` · `THE THIRD OF THREE JEWELS.` · `MONKS, NUNS, LAYMEN, LAYWOMEN.` · `NOT HALF. THE WHOLE.` · then, large: `YOU NEED PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds. Bring to mind the people who walk with you. Not the whole world, just a few faces. The friend who checks in. The teacher who believed in you. Maybe the stranger who sat near you once, in a quiet room. Hold each face for a breath or two. Notice that you didn't get here alone. If you like, let a little metta go to each of them. The bell holds the time.
The sangha. The community, the third jewel; the people who practice together and keep each other walking. Seventeenth word.
Your line: you need people. Today, message one person who helps you keep going, and tell them so, plainly. Day seventeen.

18.title: the Buddha's past lives as animals
18.hook: the Buddha's past lives as animals; the monkey king
18.carry: the bridge he made of his body
18.howItsDone: Buddhists tell the Jataka stories to children, perform them in dance and drama, paint them on temple walls, and hear them in sermons; in Theravada countries the last ten Jatakas are especially loved, and the Vessantara Jataka is staged at festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sangha, the community, the third jewel. Your line was you need people. Did you tell someone they help you keep going? Day eighteen.

A huge mango tree grows on the bank of a river. In it lives a troop of monkeys, eighty thousand of them, the story says, and their king. One night a human king's archers surround the tree. They mean to shoot every monkey at dawn. There's no way down. The monkeys are trapped between the arrows and the river. And the monkey king looks across the water at the far bank, and makes a decision. This is one of hundreds of stories Buddhists have told children, and grown-ups, for more than two thousand years. The monkey king, they say, was the Buddha.
screen: `A MANGO TREE BY A RIVER.` → `ARCHERS WAITING FOR DAWN.` → `THE MONKEY KING DECIDES.`

segments.voice: The Jataka. The word means birth stories. They're tales of the Buddha's earlier lives, before he became the Buddha, when he was still on the long way. Buddhist tradition says he lived countless lives, as kings and merchants and poor men, and very often as animals: a hare, a deer, an elephant, a quail, a monkey. The Pali collection has around five hundred and fifty of them, and they're carved in stone on some of the oldest Buddhist monuments in India. Here's the monkey king's story, the way it's told. He leaps across the river to the far bank and ties one end of a long cane to a tree. He ties the other end around his own waist and leaps back. But the cane is too short. He can reach the mango tree only with his hands. So he grips a branch and stretches his body out across the gap. And he tells his monkeys: cross. One by one, all of them run across the cane, and over his back, to safety. His body is torn by it. The human king has watched the whole thing from below. He's so moved that he has the monkey king gently brought down and cared for. And before he dies, the monkey king teaches him what a ruler is for: a king should care for his people the way I cared for mine. Each Jataka ends by telling you who was who, and in this one the monkey king was the future Buddha. Why tell stories like this? Because they show the path from the inside. Generosity. Courage. Compassion. Not as ideas, but as a monkey holding on to a branch until the last one is across.
screen: `JATAKA — BIRTH STORIES.` · `HARE, DEER, ELEPHANT, MONKEY.` · `THE CANE TOO SHORT.` · `A KING LEARNS WHAT RULING IS FOR.` · then, large: `THE BRIDGE HE MADE OF HIS BODY.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds. Think of someone who was a bridge for you. Someone who held on, stretched, maybe got a bit torn up, so you could get across something: a hard year, a move, an exam, an illness. Picture their face. Feel what they carried for you. Then, gently, ask whether there's someone you're a bridge for right now. You don't need to answer. Just let both be here. The bell holds the time.
The Jataka. Birth stories: the Buddha's past lives, many as animals, showing the path from the inside. Eighteenth word.
Your line: the bridge he made of his body. Today, thank someone who was a bridge for you, even if they don't know it. Day eighteen.

19.title: upekkha
19.hook: upekkha; the steady mind in a storm
19.carry: let it be as it is
19.tomorrow: the string too tight snaps, too loose won't play
19.howItsDone: Buddhists cultivate upekkha as one of the four brahmaviharas, often after metta, karuna and mudita, by reflecting that beings meet the results of their own actions, and by practicing steadiness through life's gains and losses.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Jataka, the monkey king. Your line was the bridge he made of his body. Did you thank someone who was a bridge for you? Day nineteen.
screen: `THE JATAKA — THE BRIDGE HE MADE OF HIS BODY.`

segments.voice: Monday, your boss says your work is brilliant. You float all day. Tuesday, a client says it's the worst thing they've seen. You don't sleep. Wednesday, a friend forgets your birthday. Thursday, a stranger compliments your coat, and suddenly it's fine again. Up, down, up, down, like a boat in weather. Most of us live like that, and we call it being human. It is. But the Buddha named those winds, one by one, and taught a way to stand in them without being blown over. Today, the steady mind in a storm.
screen: `MONDAY: BRILLIANT.` → `TUESDAY: THE WORST.` → `A BOAT IN WEATHER.`

segments.voice: Upekkha. Equanimity. It's the fourth of the divine abodes you met with karuna: friendliness, compassion, gladness, and this. The word comes from a root meaning to look, with a prefix meaning over or near. To look on, from a steady place. Not to look away. The Buddha named eight worldly winds, four pairs that blow through every life. Gain and loss. Fame and disgrace. Praise and blame. Pleasure and pain. Nobody gets only half of each pair. Everyone gets all eight. The winds aren't the problem. Getting flung around by them is. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, has the picture: "As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise." A rock. The wind still blows. The rock still feels it. It just doesn't move. Here's the most important thing about upekkha, and the easiest to get wrong. Equanimity isn't indifference. The old teachers warned that indifference is its near enemy, the thing that looks like it but isn't. Indifference says, I don't care. Equanimity says, I care, and I'm not going to be knocked over. That's why it's the last of the four. Metta wishes well. Karuna stays with pain. Mudita is glad for others. And upekkha keeps all of that steady, so the caring doesn't burn you out. Think of a good nurse, a good parent, a good friend in an emergency. Warm, and calm. That's upekkha. Letting things be as they are, and still showing up.
screen: `UPEKKHA — LOOKING ON, STEADY.` · `EIGHT WORLDLY WINDS.` · `THE ROCK IN THE WIND.` · `NOT INDIFFERENCE.` · then, large: `LET IT BE AS IT IS.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds. Sit tall and steady, like a rock on a hillside. Now let one wind blow: remember a moment of praise. Notice what it does in your body. Let it pass. Now let the other blow: a moment of blame. Notice that too. Let it pass. Come back to the breath, and to the weight of your body on the seat. The winds come and go. You stay. The bell holds the time.
Equanimity. Upekkha: looking on from a steady place, a rock in the eight winds. Caring, and not knocked over. Nineteenth word.
Your line: let it be as it is. Today, when praise or blame comes, take one breath before you react, and feel your feet on the ground. Day nineteen.

20.title: the string too tight snaps, too loose won't play
20.hook: the string too tight snaps, too loose won't play
20.howItsDone: Buddhists speak of the middle way as the path between sensual indulgence and self-mortification, and apply it to everyday practice, balancing effort and ease in meditation, eating, sleep and work.

segments.voice: Yesterday: equanimity, upekkha, the rock in the eight winds. Your line was let it be as it is. Did you take a breath before reacting? Day twenty.
screen: `EQUANIMITY — LET IT BE AS IT IS.`

segments.voice: There's a young monk named Sona, and he is trying so hard. He's been practicing walking meditation, the kind you learned about a few days ago, so intensely and for so long that his feet are bleeding. The path he walks is stained with it. And he's getting nowhere. Sitting alone, he starts to think about quitting. Going home. Using his family's money to do some good in the world instead. The Buddha hears about it and comes to see him. And he doesn't say try harder. He doesn't say give up. He asks about music.
screen: `SONA TRIES SO HARD.` → `HIS FEET ARE BLEEDING.` → `THE BUDDHA ASKS ABOUT MUSIC.`

segments.voice: Before he was a monk, Sona was skilled at the lute, a stringed instrument. So the Buddha asks him: when the strings were too tight, did the lute play well? No. When the strings were too loose, did it play well? No. And when they were neither too tight nor too loose, but tuned just right? Then it played beautifully. It's the same with effort, the Buddha says. Too much, and you become restless and strained. Too little, and you become lazy. Find the right tuning. Sona takes the advice, and the story says that before long, he reaches awakening. This is the middle way, and it's where the Buddha's whole teaching began. Remember the first sermon, in the deer park? Before he taught the four truths, he told his five companions there are two extremes to avoid. On one side, chasing pleasure: the life he'd had in the palace. On the other, punishing the body: the years he'd spent nearly starving himself as a seeker. Both, he said, lead nowhere good. Between them runs a middle way, and that middle way is the eightfold path you already know. So the middle way isn't a bland compromise, halfway between two things. It's more like tuning. A string that's in tune isn't half-tight. It's exactly right for that string, that instrument, that day. And it needs retuning, again and again, because strings drift. Some days you need more effort. Some days you need rest. The skill isn't finding the answer once. It's listening, and adjusting.
screen: `TOO TIGHT, TOO LOOSE, TUNED.` · `EFFORT, THE SAME WAY.` · `TWO EXTREMES TO AVOID.` · `NOT HALFWAY. TUNED.` · then, large: `THE MIDDLE WAY.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds. Sit, and check your tuning. Is your body too tight? Clenched jaw, raised shoulders, gripping hands? Let a little go. Is it too loose? Slumped, drowsy, drifting? Lift the chest a little and brighten your attention. Look for the place in between: upright and relaxed, awake and easy. When you drift one way or the other, gently retune. The bell holds the time.
The middle way. Between indulgence and self-punishment, not a compromise but a tuning, adjusted again and again. Twentieth word.
Your line: tune. Today, notice one thing you're doing too hard, or too little. Adjust it by one notch, and see how it plays. Day twenty.

21.title: the mountain ahead
21.hook: the mountain ahead; "mind is the forerunner"
21.howItsDone: Buddhists, especially in Theravada countries, memorize and chant verses of the Dhammapada, hear them explained in sermons with the stories that go with each verse, and keep a copy at home as a small book of daily wisdom.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the middle way, the lute string tuned just right. Your line was tune. What did you adjust by one notch? Day twenty-one.

Three weeks. Look at your strand. Metta. The breath. Dukkha. The Buddha. Four noble truths. Sati, the bell, anicca, anatta. The precepts, dana, walking meditation. Karuna, the sangha, the Jataka. Equanimity, the middle way. Twenty words, the everyday vocabulary of a Buddhist life. Those are the foothills. Tomorrow the path starts climbing: the Buddha's whole life, told like a serial, from a queen's dream to his last words. So today, from the top of the foothills, we look up at the mountain. One small book that has walked into more languages and pockets than almost any other Buddhist text.
screen: `TWENTY WORDS ON YOUR STRAND.` → `THE FOOTHILLS, DONE.` → `THE MOUNTAIN AHEAD.`

segments.voice: The Dhammapada. Four hundred and twenty-three short verses, in twenty-six chapters, kept in the Pali canon and remembered as the Buddha's own sayings. Many Buddhists learn verses by heart as children. Monks chant it. And it was one of the first Buddhist texts ever put into English. The name has two halves. Dhamma, the teaching, the way things are. And pada, which means a foot, a step, a path, and also a line of verse. So it's the path of the teaching, or the verses of the teaching, and both are right. Every step is a line. You've already met it five times in these three weeks: hatred ceasing by love, the eightfold way as the best of ways, the rock in the wind. Now here's where it starts. The very first verse. Modern translators render it something like: mind is the forerunner of all things. In Max Müller's translation from eighteen eighty-one it reads: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts." Then two images. If someone speaks or acts from a harmful mind, pain follows, like the wheel of a cart following the ox's foot. And if someone speaks or acts from a clear, good mind, happiness follows them, in Müller's words, "like a shadow that never leaves him." Notice what the first verse is doing. It isn't telling you what to believe about the universe. It's pointing you back at your own mind, the one place you can actually start. The whole path you've walked so far, the breath, the noticing, the metta, begins right there.
screen: `423 VERSES, 26 CHAPTERS.` · `DHAMMA + PADA: TEACHING, STEP.` · `MIND IS THE FORERUNNER.` · `THE WHEEL, AND THE SHADOW.` · then, large: `WHAT YOU THINK, YOU BECOME.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds. Think back over these three weeks. Let the words drift past: the wish for someone's good, the breath, the wobble, the bell, the passing leaf, the open hand, the monkey on the branch. Don't try to remember them all. Just notice which one has stuck. Which came back to you on an ordinary day, without being asked? Hold that one word. Breathe with it. It's yours now. The bell holds the time.
The Dhammapada. The path of the teaching, verses of the teaching: four hundred and twenty-three lines that start with the mind. Twenty-first word, and camp one is done.
Your line: what you think, you become. Today, catch one thought you keep repeating, and ask what it's making of you. Tomorrow, the story begins. Day twenty-one.

what a scholar hears: the Dhammapada sits in the Khuddaka Nikaya; Max Müller's 1881 translation (Sacred Books of the East X) rendered verse 1 very freely as 'all that we are is the result of what we have thought.'
